title: A Lawsuit Claims AI, Not People, Picked Who Meta Laid Off
hook: Being screened by AI isn't just about getting hired — a new lawsuit claims Meta used AI-driven performance data to decide who to fire, allegedly targeting workers on medical leave.
key_points: Ars Technica and The Verge report 26 former Meta employees are suing over layoff decisions.
The suit claims Meta used a 'constellation' of internal AI tools to score and target workers.
It alleges the targeting disproportionately hit employees on leave for disabilities or illness.
Meta denies using AI to terminate workers with disabilities and medical problems.
It's a mirror image of AI hiring screens — the same automated scoring, now used to decide who goes.
content_html: Most conversations about being "judged by AI" focus on getting in the door — a résumé screener, a loan algorithm. A new lawsuit reported by Ars Technica and The Verge points to the other end of the employment relationship: getting pushed out. Twenty-six former Meta employees are suing the company, alleging that its layoff decisions were driven by AI rather than human judgment.
extra_html: The complaint claims Meta drew on a "constellation" of internal AI tools that tracked employee performance data, and that this scoring system disproportionately targeted workers who were on leave for disabilities or medical conditions — exactly the kind of protected group anti-discrimination law exists to shield. Meta denies using AI to terminate workers because of disabilities or medical problems, and the underlying facts will be argued out in court. But the shape of the allegation is instructive regardless of how the case resolves: the same automated scoring systems praised for making hiring "faster and more consistent" can, in principle, make the opposite decision just as opaquely — who to let go, with a model rather than a manager doing the sorting. If you work somewhere that uses performance analytics tools, it's a reminder that the questions worth asking about AI hiring screens — what data feeds the score, who can see it, what recourse exists — apply just as much on the way out.

flashcards.prompt: What does the lawsuit against Meta allege about its layoff process?

choices.text: That AI tools scored workers and disproportionately targeted those on medical leave
That Meta refused to use any automated tools in its layoffs
That the layoffs were randomly generated by a lottery

flashcards.explanation_html: Per the reporting, former employees allege Meta used internal AI performance tools to determine who to lay off, and that this disproportionately hit workers on leave for disabilities or medical issues. Meta denies this.

flashcards.prompt: How does this case relate to AI screening job applicants?
flashcards.back_html: It's the same basic risk in reverse — instead of an algorithm deciding who gets hired, one allegedly helped decide who gets let go, with the same concerns about opaque scoring and hidden bias.
